sections.h2: Selling a house in Hamilton Township, Mercer County
sections.html:
Three items control the schedule here: a Certificate of Approval from the township's housing inspectors, a settled tax balance, and a deed recorded in Trenton. This page covers the Hamilton beside Trenton, a separate place from the Atlantic County township of the same name.

Hamilton is the most populous municipality in Mercer County, with an estimated 94,157 residents. About 71.6 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and the typical value is $335,500. A buyer who pays cash and accepts the house as it stands drops the loan approval and repair requests that often stretch out an ordinary sale.

sections.h2: Neighborhoods and what buyers look for
sections.html:
Hamilton covers 39.44 square miles and is the largest suburb of Trenton, which lies to its west. It has no true downtown. Separate communities act as commercial centers instead: Mercerville (13,447 residents in 2020), Hamilton Square (12,679), White Horse (9,791), Yardville (6,965) and Groveville (3,106).

Open space is a draw. A 350-acre township park, and Mercer County Park's 2,500 acres adjoin it to the north. Retirement communities and assisted-living facilities have gone up near Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital Hamilton, and new restaurants, banks and stores have opened along Route 33.

The Postal Service officially treats many Hamilton addresses as Trenton, so use the township name in your advertising. That way buyers can find the right tax and school information.

The average home here was billed $8,069 in 2025, and the 618 homes sold in the state's study averaged $404,824. Recent nearby closings tell you more about price than any average does.

The 2025 general rate for the township is 3.708 per $100, and the effective rate is 2.434. Sale prices run well above assessments, so do not treat the assessed value as your asking price.

Before any change in occupancy of a house or apartment, the Office of Housing Inspection and Landlord Compliance has to issue a Certificate of Approval. It confirms the building and premises meet township ordinances, and life safety comes first in the inspection.

You apply through the Change of Occupancy Application Portal or on paper at the office. A Change of Occupancy Checklist is published, and reading it before the inspector arrives is the cheapest way to avoid a second visit. The township does not test houses for lead on request, so a seller who wants a lead test must hire a private inspector.

  • Apply once you have a signed contract so the approval is fresh at closing.
  • Check smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, since state rules require a certificate valid for six months on one-family and two-family sales.
  • Fix visible safety problems, such as loose rails and missing detectors, before the appointment.

The construction office keeps a house's blueprints for 10 years, so ask for plans if you need to show a buyer what was built. The Land Use Office can confirm a parcel's zoning designation.

The Mercer County Board of Taxation, at 640 South Broad Street in Trenton, certifies assessments and hears appeals. Regular appeals are due April 1, and appeals over added or omitted assessments are due December 1. In-person filing runs from 8:30 a.m. until 4:00 p.m.

Postcards with the new assessment go out at the end of January, so read yours before deciding to file. The county's Property Information Portal shows property record cards, sales, deeds and tax information, which helps you find comparable sales near your street. Ask the township collector for a written tax payoff before closing.

sections.h2: Seller costs and the Mercer County Clerk
sections.html:
The seller pays New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. For a price above $350,000 the rate starts at $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000, and the schedule steps up in higher brackets. The county clerk adds that deeds above $1,000,000 recorded since July 10, 2025 carry a revised fee under a new state law.

Deeds are recorded at the Mercer County Clerk's Office, 209 South Broad Street in Trenton, where title searchers and the public can view a property's history in the records room or online. Resident sellers sign the GIT/REP-3 residency certification. Sellers who live elsewhere prepay Gross Income Tax of 2 percent of the price or more.

  • State transfer fee, set by the rate table.
  • Mortgage and lien payoffs.
  • The seller's share of the quarter's property tax.
  • Certificate and inspection fees set by the township.

About 28 percent of occupied homes in Hamilton are rented, and typical rent is $1,634. The same housing inspection office that approves owner sales handles any change of occupancy in a house, dwelling unit or apartment. A rental passing to a new tenant or a new owner goes through it too.

Gather leases, move-out dates and repair records before you apply. A buyer who plans to keep renting the house will need approval for the next tenancy, so a clean inspection record helps the sale.

sections.h2: Walking a cash sale through the steps
sections.html:
With no lender involved, your to-do list is short. Book the occupancy inspection as soon as a contract is signed, fix any safety items it lists, and request the tax payoff from the collector. Then meet the closing attorney or title company to sign the deed and the residency or prepayment forms. The deed goes to the clerk's office on South Broad Street.

Bring your deed, a recent tax bill, any mortgage payoff statement, leases if tenants live there, and the keys. If taxes are owed, the amount is taken from your proceeds at closing, so you do not have to pay it beforehand. Water comes from Aqua New Jersey or Trenton Water Works, so confirm which utility serves the house and have a final reading arranged.

Hamilton is the only New Jersey municipality hosting Interstate 95 along with both of its auxiliary routes, I-195 and I-295, plus U.S. Routes 130 and 206 and Routes 29, 33 and 156. The township lies about 65 miles from New York City and 35 miles from Philadelphia. The Hamilton station on Sloan Avenue, off I-295 Exit 65B, serves NJ Transit's Northeast Corridor, so commuters make up a real share of buyers.

faqs.q: Which approval must a seller get in Hamilton Township, Mercer County?
faqs.a: A Certificate of Approval from the Office of Housing Inspection and Landlord Compliance, required before a change of occupancy. Apply through the township portal or with the office's paper forms.

faqs.q: Where is an assessment appeal filed in Hamilton Township?
faqs.a: With the Mercer County Board of Taxation at 640 South Broad Street in Trenton by April 1. Appeals over added or omitted assessments are due December 1.

faqs.q: Will the township test my house for lead before a sale?
faqs.a: No, it does not test houses for lead on request. A seller who wants a test has to hire a private inspector.

faqs.q: Which office records a Hamilton Township deed?
faqs.a: The Mercer County Clerk's Office at 209 South Broad Street in Trenton. Deeds above $1,000,000 recorded since July 10, 2025 carry a revised fee under the new state law.

faqs.q: Why do some Hamilton addresses say Trenton?
faqs.a: The Postal Service officially treats many Hamilton addresses as Trenton even though the house is in Hamilton Township. Name the township in your listing so buyers can find the right tax and school information.
